claim: Schnyder corneal dystrophy (SCD) is characterized by corneal opacification owing to overaccumulation of cholesterol.
source: Autosomal-dominant Schnyder corneal dystrophy (SCD) is characterized by corneal opacification owing to overaccumulation of cholesterol.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established characteristic of SCD.

claim: SCD is caused by mutations in UBIAD1.
source: SCD is caused by mutations in UBIAD1, which utilizes geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate (GGpp) to synthesize vitamin K2.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: UBIAD1 utilizes geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate (GGpp) to synthesize vitamin K2.
source: SCD is caused by mutations in UBIAD1, which utilizes geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate (GGpp) to synthesize vitamin K2.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Sterols trigger binding of UBIAD1 to HMGCR, thereby inhibiting its endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-associated degradation (ERAD).
source: Using cultured cells, we previously showed that sterols trigger binding of UBIAD1 to the cholesterol biosynthetic enzyme HMG CoA reductase (HMGCR), thereby inhibiting its endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-associated degradation (ERAD) (Schumacher et al. 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and references a previous publication by the authors.

claim: GGpp triggers release of UBIAD1 from HMGCR, allowing maximal ERAD and ER-to-Golgi transport of UBIAD1.
source: GGpp triggers release of UBIAD1 from HMGCR, allowing maximal ERAD and ER-to-Golgi transport of UBIAD1.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from previous work.

claim: SCD-associated UBIAD1 resists GGpp-induced release and is sequestered in ER to inhibit ERAD.
source: SCD-associated UBIAD1 resists GGpp-induced release and is sequestered in ER to inhibit ERAD.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from previous work.

claim: Knockin mice expressing SCD-associated UBIAD1 accumulate HMGCR in several tissues resulting from ER sequestration of mutant UBIAD1 and inhibition of HMGCR ERAD.
source: We now report knockin mice expressing SCD-associated UBIAD1 accumulate HMGCR in several tissues resulting from ER sequestration of mutant UBIAD1 and inhibition of HMGCR ERAD.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 1-6.

claim: Corneas from aged knockin mice exhibit signs of opacification and sterol overaccumulation.
source: Corneas from aged knockin mice exhibit signs of opacification and sterol overaccumulation.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 7.

claim: Inhibition of HMGCR ERAD contributes to SCD pathogenesis.
source: These results establish the physiological significance of UBIAD1 in cholesterol homeostasis and indicate inhibition of HMGCR ERAD contributes to SCD pathogenesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Mutations in the gene encoding UBIAD1 cause Schnyder corneal dystrophy (SCD).
source: Mutations in the gene encoding UbiA prenyltransferase domain-containing protein-1 (UBIAD1) cause Schnyder corneal dystrophy (SCD), a rare autosomal dominant eye disease characterized by opacification of the cornea (Klintworth, 2009; Weiss, 2009; Orr et al., 2007; Weiss et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: SCD is a rare autosomal dominant eye disease characterized by opacification of the cornea.
source: Mutations in the gene encoding UbiA prenyltransferase domain-containing protein-1 (UBIAD1) cause Schnyder corneal dystrophy (SCD), a rare autosomal dominant eye disease characterized by opacification of the cornea (Klintworth, 2009; Weiss, 2009; Orr et al., 2007; Weiss et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Corneal opacification associated with SCD progresses slowly with age and ultimately leads to reduced visual acuity.
source: Although apparent early in life, corneal opacification associated with SCD progresses slowly with age and ultimately leads to reduced visual acuity.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an established characteristic of SCD.

claim: Corneal transplant surgery is utilized for treatment of SCD in 50% of SCD patients > 50 years of age.
source: The severity of visual impairment is underscored by the frequency in which corneal transplant surgery is utilized for treatment of SCD, which rises from 50% in SCD patients > 50 years of age to more than 70% for those 70 years and older (Weiss, 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Corneal transplant surgery is utilized for treatment of SCD in more than 70% of SCD patients 70 years and older.
source: The severity of visual impairment is underscored by the frequency in which corneal transplant surgery is utilized for treatment of SCD, which rises from 50% in SCD patients > 50 years of age to more than 70% for those 70 years and older (Weiss, 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Corneas from SCD patients exhibit a marked accumulation of cholesterol.
source: Biochemical analyses of corneas from SCD patients revealed a marked accumulation of cholesterol (McCarthy et al., 1994; Gaynor et al., 1996; Yamada et al., 1998), suggesting that dysregulation of cholesterol metabolism significantly contributes to the pathogenesis of SCD.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Dysregulation of cholesterol metabolism significantly contributes to the pathogenesis of SCD.
source: Biochemical analyses of corneas from SCD patients revealed a marked accumulation of cholesterol (McCarthy et al., 1994; Gaynor et al., 1996; Yamada et al., 1998), suggesting that dysregulation of cholesterol metabolism significantly contributes to the pathogenesis of SCD.
evidence: This is stated as a suggestion based on biochemical analyses cited in the introduction.

claim: Systemic hypercholesterolemia has been reported to be associated with some, but not all cases of SCD.
source: Systemic hypercholesterolemia has been reported to be associated with some, but not all cases of the disease (Thiel et al., 1977; Brownstein et al., 1991; Crispin, 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: UBIAD1 belongs to the UbiA superfamily of integral membrane prenyltransferases.
source: UBIAD1 belongs to the UbiA superfamily of integral membrane prenyltransferases that catalyze transfer of isoprenyl groups to aromatic acceptors, generating a wide variety of molecules ranging from ubiquinones, chlorophylls, and hemes to vitamin E and vitamin K (Li, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: UbiA superfamily prenyltransferases catalyze transfer of isoprenyl groups to aromatic acceptors, generating molecules including ubiquinones, chlorophylls, hemes, vitamin E and vitamin K.
source: UBIAD1 belongs to the UbiA superfamily of integral membrane prenyltransferases that catalyze transfer of isoprenyl groups to aromatic acceptors, generating a wide variety of molecules ranging from ubiquinones, chlorophylls, and hemes to vitamin E and vitamin K (Li, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: UBIAD1 mediates transfer of the 20-carbon geranylgeranyl moiety from geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate (GGpp) to menadione (vitamin K3) released from plant-derived phylloquinone (vitamin K1), generating the vitamin K2 subtype menaquinone-4 (MK-4).
source: UBIAD1 mediates transfer of the 20-carbon geranylgeranyl moiety from geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate (GGpp) to menadione (vitamin K3) released from plant-derived phylloquinone (vitamin K1), generating the vitamin K2 subtype menaquinone-4 (MK-4) (Nakagawa et al., 2010; Hirota et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: 25 missense mutations that alter 21 amino acids in the UBIAD1 protein have been identified in SCD families.
source: To date, 25 missense mutations that alter 21 amino acids in the UBIAD1 protein have been identified in SCD families.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a summary of known mutations.

claim: Residues corresponding to SCD-associated mutations in human UBIAD1 cluster around the active site of the enzyme.
source: Structural analyses of archaeal UbiA prenyltransferases revealed that residues corresponding to SCD-associated mutations in human UBIAD1 cluster around the active site of the enzyme (Cheng and Li, 2014; Huang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: All SCD-associated variants of UBIAD1 are defective in mediating synthesis of MK-4.
source: Indeed, all SCD-associated variants of UBIAD1 are defective in mediating synthesis of MK-4 (Hirota et al., 2015; Jun, D.-J. and DeBose-Boyd, R.A., unpublished observations)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations and unpublished observations.

claim: For some SCD-associated UBIAD1 variants, the defect in MK-4 synthesis likely results from reduced affinity for GGpp.
source: Indeed, all SCD-associated variants of UBIAD1 are defective in mediating synthesis of MK-4 (Hirota et al., 2015; Jun, D.-J. and DeBose-Boyd, R.A., unpublished observations) and for some variants, this defect likely results from reduced affinity for GGpp.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a likely explanation based on inference.

claim: UBIAD1 associates with the endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-localized enzyme HMGCR.
source: The first link between UBIAD1 and cholesterol metabolism was provided by the discovery of its association with the endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-localized enzyme 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl coenzyme A reductase (HMGCR) (Nickerson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: HMGCR catalyzes reduction of HMG CoA to mevalonate, a reaction that constitutes the rate-limiting step in synthesis of cholesterol and the essential nonsterol isoprenoids GGpp and farnesyl pyrophosphate (Fpp).
source: HMGCR catalyzes reduction of HMG CoA to mevalonate, a reaction that constitutes the rate-limiting step in synthesis of cholesterol and the essential nonsterol isoprenoids GGpp and farnesyl pyrophosphate (Fpp) (Goldstein and Brown, 1990; Wang and Casey, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Fpp and GGpp can become transferred to many cellular proteins and are utilized in synthesis of other nonsterol isoprenoids including ubiquinone, heme, dolichol, and MK-4.
source: Fpp and GGpp can become transferred to many cellular proteins and are utilized in synthesis of other nonsterol isoprenoids including ubiquinone, heme, dolichol, and MK-4.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: HMGCR is subjected to tight feedback control through transcriptional and post-transcriptional mechanisms mediated by sterol and nonsterol isoprenoids.
source: HMGCR is subjected to tight feedback control through transcriptional and post-transcriptional mechanisms mediated by sterol and nonsterol isoprenoids (Brown and Goldstein, 1980).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Sterols mediate transcriptional effects on HMGCR by inhibiting proteolytic activation of membrane-bound transcription factors called sterol regulatory element-binding proteins (SREBPs).
source: Sterols mediate the transcriptional effects by inhibiting proteolytic activation of membrane-bound transcription factors called sterol regulatory element-binding proteins (SREBPs).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: SREBPs enhance transcription of genes encoding HMGCR and other cholesterol biosynthetic enzymes as well as the low density lipoprotein (LDL) receptor.
source: SREBPs enhance transcription of genes encoding HMGCR and other cholesterol biosynthetic enzymes as well as the low density lipoprotein (LDL) receptor that removes cholesterol-rich LDL from circulation (Horton et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Post-transcriptional regulation of HMGCR is mediated by sterol and nonsterol isoprenoids, which combine to accelerate the ER-associated degradation (ERAD) of HMGCR through a reaction that involves the 26S proteasome.
source: Post-transcriptional regulation of HMGCR is mediated by sterol and nonsterol isoprenoids, which combine to accelerate the ER-associated degradation (ERAD) of HMGCR through a reaction that involves the 26S proteasome (Nakanishi et al., 1988; Ravid et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Accumulation of sterols in ER membranes triggers binding of HMGCR to ER membrane proteins called Insigs.
source: Our group discovered that accumulation of sterols in ER membranes triggers binding of HMGCR to ER membrane proteins called Insigs (Sever et al., 2003a; Sever et al., 2003b).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Ubiquitination of HMGCR by Insig-associated ubiquitin ligases marks the enzyme for extraction across ER membranes and release into the cytosol for proteasome-mediated ERAD.
source: Subsequent ubiquitination of HMGCR by Insig-associated ubiquitin ligases (Song et al., 2005; Jo et al., 2011; Jiang et al., 2018) mark the enzyme for extraction across ER membranes and release into the cytosol for proteasome-mediated ERAD (Elsabrouty et al., 2013; Morris et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: GGpp augments ERAD of ubiquitinated HMGCR by enhancing its membrane extraction.
source: GGpp augments ERAD of ubiquitinated HMGCR by enhancing its membrane extraction (Elsabrouty et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Sterols cause a subset of HMGCR molecules to bind to UBIAD1, which protects HMGCR from accelerated ERAD.
source: Recently, we discovered that sterols also cause a subset of HMGCR molecules to bind to UBIAD1 (32). This binding protects HMGCR from accelerated ERAD, permitting continued synthesis of nonsterol isoprenoids even when cellular sterols are abundant (Schumacher et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Binding of UBIAD1 to HMGCR permits continued synthesis of nonsterol isoprenoids even when cellular sterols are abundant.
source: This binding protects HMGCR from accelerated ERAD, permitting continued synthesis of nonsterol isoprenoids even when cellular sterols are abundant (Schumacher et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Eliminating expression of UBIAD1 relieves the GGpp requirement for HMGCR ERAD, indicating the reaction is inhibited by UBIAD1.
source: Eliminating expression of UBIAD1 relieves the GGpp requirement for HMGCR ERAD, indicating the reaction is inhibited by UBIAD1.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a finding from previous work.

claim: UBIAD1 continuously cycles between the ER and Golgi despite its steady-state Golgi localization in GGpp-replete cells.
source: Further characterization revealed that despite its steady-state Golgi localization in GGpp-replete cells, UBIAD1 continuously cycles between the ER and Golgi.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a finding from previous work.

claim: Upon sensing depletion of GGpp in membranes of the ER, UBIAD1 becomes trapped in the organelle and inhibits ERAD of HMGCR to stimulate synthesis of mevalonate for replenishment of GGpp.
source: Upon sensing depletion of GGpp in membranes of the ER, UBIAD1 becomes trapped in the organelle and inhibits ERAD of HMGCR to stimulate synthesis of mevalonate for replenishment of GGpp.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a finding from previous work.

claim: SCD-associated UBIAD1 inhibits HMGCR ERAD in a dominant-negative fashion, leading to a marked increase in synthesis and intracellular accumulation of cholesterol.
source: The ensuing inhibition of HMGCR ERAD, which occurs in a dominant-negative fashion, leads to a marked increase in synthesis and intracellular accumulation of cholesterol (Schumacher et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The N100S mutation in mouse UBIAD1 corresponds to the SCD-associated UBIAD1 (N102S) mutation in the human enzyme.
source: The N100S mutation in mouse UBIAD1 corresponds to the SCD-associated UBIAD1 (N102S) mutation in the human enzyme.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: Livers of male Ubiad1WT/Ki and Ubiad1Ki/Ki mice consuming chow diet ad libitum exhibited a noticeable increase (1.8- and 5.2-fold, respectively) in the amount of HMGCR protein compared to that in WT littermates.
source: Immunoblot analysis revealed that livers of male Ubiad1WT/Ki and Ubiad1Ki/Ki mice consuming chow diet ad libitum exhibited a noticeable increase (1.8- and 5.2-fold, respectively) in the amount of HMGCR protein compared to that in WT littermates (Figure 1B, lanes 1–3).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The amount of Hmgcr mRNA was reduced approximately 40% in knockin mice.
source: However, the amount of Hmgcr mRNA was reduced approximately 40% in knockin mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: UBIAD1 (N100S) protein accumulated in livers of heterozygous and homozygous Ubiad1 knockin mice.
source: UBIAD1 (N100S) protein also accumulated in livers of heterozygous and homozygous Ubiad1 knockin mice (Figure 1B, lanes 1–3)
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Accumulation of UBIAD1 (N100S) protein in knockin mice was not accompanied by an increase in hepatic Ubiad1 mRNA.
source: however, this was not accompanied by an increase in hepatic Ubiad1 mRNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Levels of nuclear SREBP-1 and SREBP-2 were reduced in livers of Ubiad1WT/Ki and Ubiad1Ki/Ki mice.
source: Levels of nuclear SREBP-1 (Figure 1B, lanes 4–6) and SREBP-2 (lanes 7–9) were reduced in livers of Ubiad1WT/Ki and Ubiad1Ki/Ki mice
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Reduced levels of nuclear SREBPs in knockin mice coincided with reduced expression of mRNAs encoding SREBP target genes.
source: which coincided with reduced expression of mRNAs encoding SREBP target genes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Cholesterol was slightly, but significantly increased in Ubiad1Ki/Ki livers.
source: Cholesterol was slightly, but significantly increased in Ubiad1Ki/Ki livers
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by biochemical assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Plasma cholesterol, triglycerides, and non-esterified fatty acids as well as liver triglycerides were not significantly changed between WT and Ubiad1Ki/Ki mice.
source: however, plasma cholesterol, triglycerides, and non-esterified fatty acids as well as liver triglycerides were not significantly changed between the groups of animals (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by biochemical assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Male Ubiad1WT/Ki and Ubiad1Ki/Ki mice on the BL6 background accumulated hepatic HMGCR and UBIAD1 proteins.
source: The results shown in Figure 2A reveal that male Ubiad1WT/Ki and Ubiad1Ki/Ki mice on the BL6 background accumulated hepatic HMGCR and UBIAD1 proteins (lanes 1–3)
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Levels of nuclear SREBP-1 were unchanged in livers of Ubiad1Ki/Ki mice on the BL6 background.
source: whereas levels of nuclear SREBP-1 and SREBP-2 were either unchanged (nuclear SREBP-1, lanes 4–6)
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Levels of nuclear SREBP-2 were reduced in livers of Ubiad1Ki/Ki mice on the BL6 background.
source: or reduced (nuclear SREBP-2, lanes 7–9).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: HMGCR and UBIAD1 proteins accumulated to varying degrees in eyes, kidneys, brains, testes, spleens, and pancreas of Ubiad1Ki/Ki mice.
source: HMGCR and UBIAD1 proteins accumulated and Hmgcr mRNA was down-regulated to varying degrees in other tissues of the knockin mice (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunoblot and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: Hmgcr mRNA was down-regulated to varying degrees in eyes, kidneys, brains, testes, spleens, and pancreas of Ubiad1Ki/Ki mice.
source: HMGCR and UBIAD1 proteins accumulated and Hmgcr mRNA was down-regulated to varying degrees in other tissues of the knockin mice (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunoblot and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: HMGCR and UBIAD1 protein accumulated to a similar extent in livers and eyes of female C57BL/6J Ubiad1Ki/Ki mice.
source: HMGCR and UBIAD1 protein accumulated to a similar extent in livers and eyes of female C57BL/6J Ubiad1Ki/Ki mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: WT and Ubiad1Ki/Ki mice had similar body and liver weights.
source: Table 1 shows that WT and Ubiad1Ki/Ki mice had similar body and liver weights.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Table 1.

claim: Plasma levels of triglycerides, cholesterol, and non-esterified fatty acids (NEFAs) were slightly reduced in Ubiad1Ki/Ki mice; however, these reductions were not significant.
source: Plasma levels of triglycerides, cholesterol, and non-esterified fatty acids (NEFAs) were slightly reduced in Ubiad1Ki/Ki mice; however, these reductions were not significant.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Table 1.

claim: Ubiad1Ki/Ki mice exhibited a small but significant increase in the amount of cholesterol in the liver.
source: The knockin mice exhibited a small but significant increase in the amount of cholesterol in the liver (Table 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Table 1.

claim: Levels of MK-4 were reduced 50% in livers of Ubiad1Ki/Ki mice relative to those observed in WT animals.
source: The results show that levels of MK-4 were reduced 50% relative to those observed in WT animals, despite a 4.2-fold increase in the amount of hepatic UBIAD1 protein.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 3.

claim: When normalized to the amount of UBIAD1 protein, the relative level of MK-4 was reduced by more than 80% in livers of Ubiad1Ki/Ki mice.
source: When normalized to the amount of UBIAD1 protein, we estimate the relative level of MK-4 was reduced by more than 80% in livers of Ubiad1Ki/Ki mice.
evidence: This is a calculation based on primary data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Levels of geranylgeraniol (GGOH; derived from GGpp) were significantly increased in livers of Ubiad1Ki/Ki mice.
source: In contrast to results with MK-4, levels of geranylgeraniol (GGOH; derived from GGpp) and ubiquinone-10, were significantly increased in livers of Ubiad1Ki/Ki mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Levels of ubiquinone-10 were significantly increased in livers of Ubiad1Ki/Ki mice.
source: In contrast to results with MK-4, levels of geranylgeraniol (GGOH; derived from GGpp) and ubiquinone-10, were significantly increased in livers of Ubiad1Ki/Ki mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Plant-derived phylloquinone (vitamin K1) was significantly decreased in livers of Ubiad1Ki/Ki mice.
source: This was accompanied by a small, but significant decrease in plant-derived phylloquinone (vitamin K1)
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Bacterial-derived vitamin K2 subtype menaquinone-7 (MK-7) remained unchanged in the knockin livers.
source: bacterial-derived vitamin K2 subtype menaquinone-7 (MK-7) remained unchanged in the knockin livers.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 3.

claim: MK-4 was reduced in kidneys, brains, spleens, and testes of Ubiad1Ki/Ki mice.
source: MK-4 was reduced, whereas levels of GGOH and/or ubiquinone-10 were increased in kidneys, brains, spleens, and testes of Ubiad1Ki/Ki mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Levels of GGOH and/or ubiquinone-10 were increased in kidneys, brains, spleens, and testes of Ubiad1Ki/Ki mice.
source: MK-4 was reduced, whereas levels of GGOH and/or ubiquinone-10 were increased in kidneys, brains, spleens, and testes of Ubiad1Ki/Ki mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: A low level of HMGCR and UBIAD1 protein was detected in membrane fractions isolated from WT MEFs cultured in sterol and nonsterol isoprenoid-replete medium containing fetal calf serum.
source: A low level of HMGCR and UBIAD1 protein was detected in membrane fractions isolated from WT MEFs cultured in sterol and nonsterol isoprenoid-replete medium containing fetal calf serum (Figure 4A, lane 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: HMGCR and UBIAD1 proteins markedly accumulated in MEFs derived from Ubiad1Ki/Ki mice.
source: Both proteins markedly accumulated in MEFs derived from Ubiad1Ki/Ki mice (lane 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Levels of nuclear SREBP-1 and SREBP-2 were reduced in Ubiad1Ki/Ki MEFs.
source: In contrast, levels of nuclear SREBP-1 and SREBP-2 were reduced in Ubiad1Ki/Ki MEFs (Figure 4A, compare lanes 3 and 4)
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Reduced levels of nuclear SREBPs in Ubiad1Ki/Ki MEFs is consistent with reduced levels of Hmgcr mRNA and increased levels of intracellular cholesterol.
source: which is consistent with reduced levels of Hmgcr mRNA and increased levels of intracellular cholesterol (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by qRT-PCR and cholesterol assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: 25-HC caused the disappearance of HMGCR from membranes of WT MEFs.
source: The results show that 25-HC caused the disappearance of HMGCR from membranes of WT MEFs as expected (Figure 4C, lanes 1 and 2; 5 and 6).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: 25-HC-induced disappearance of HMGCR was blunted in membranes from either Ubiad1Ki/Ki or HmgcrKi/Ki MEFs.
source: However, this disappearance was blunted in membranes from either Ubiad1Ki/Ki or HmgcrKi/Ki MEFs (lanes 3 and 4; 7 and 8).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Sterols continued to stimulate HMGCR ubiquitination in Ubiad1Ki/Ki MEFs despite resistance of HMGCR to sterol-accelerated ERAD.
source: Despite resistance of HMGCR to sterol-accelerated ERAD, the experiment of Figure 4D shows that sterols continued to stimulate HMGCR ubiquitination in Ubiad1Ki/Ki MEFs.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunoprecipitation and immunoblot data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: 25-HC caused HMGCR to become ubiquitinated in WT and Ubiad1Ki/Ki MEFs.
source: 25-HC caused HMGCR to become ubiquitinated in WT and Ubiad1Ki/Ki MEFs, as indicated by smears of reactivity in anti-ubiquitin immunoblots of the HMGCR immunoprecipitates (Figure 4D, lanes 1–6).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunoprecipitation and immunoblot data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: HMGCR resisted 25-HC-induced ubiquitination in MEFs derived from HmgcrKi/Ki mice.
source: As expected, HMGCR resisted 25-HC-induced ubiquitination in MEFs derived from HmgcrKi/Ki mice (compare lanes 7 and 8 with lanes 9–12).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunoprecipitation and immunoblot data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Cholesterol feeding led to reduced expression of HMGCR protein in membranes isolated from livers of WT mice.
source: The results show that cholesterol feeding led to reduced expression of HMGCR protein in membranes isolated from livers of WT mice (Figure 5A, lane 2)
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: A significant amount of HMGCR protein remained in hepatic membranes of cholesterol-fed Ubiad1Ki/Ki mice.
source: however, a significant amount of HMGCR protein remained in hepatic membranes of cholesterol-fed Ubiad1Ki/Ki mice (lane 4).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Cholesterol feeding reduced the amount of Insig-1 protein in livers of both WT and Ubiad1Ki/Ki mice.
source: The feeding regimen reduced the amount of Insig-1 protein (lanes 2 and 4)
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Cholesterol feeding reduced nuclear SREBP-2 in livers of both WT and Ubiad1Ki/Ki mice.
source: and nuclear SREBP-2 (lanes 6 and 8) in both WT and Ubiad1Ki/Ki livers.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Dietary cholesterol reduced mRNAs encoding HMGCR and other SREBP targets in livers of WT and Ubiad1Ki/Ki mice.
source: Dietary cholesterol also reduced mRNAs encoding HMGCR and other SREBP targets in livers of WT and Ubiad1Ki/Ki mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The membrane-bound precursor and nuclear forms of SREBP-1 were induced by cholesterol feeding in livers of both WT and Ubiad1Ki/Ki mice.
source: The membrane-bound precursor and nuclear forms of SREBP-1 were induced by cholesterol feeding in livers of both lines of mice (lanes 6 and 8).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Sterol-mediated activation of liver x receptors (LXRs) modulates expression of SREBP-1c, the major SREBP-1 isoform in the mouse liver.
source: This induction can be attributed to sterol-mediated activation of liver x receptors (LXRs) that modulate expression of SREBP-1c, the major SREBP-1 isoform in the mouse liver (Repa et al., 2000; Liang et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated as an explanation with supporting citations.

claim: The mRNAs encoding SREBP-1c and two other LXR targets, ABCG5 and ABCG8, were enhanced in WT and Ubiad1Ki/Ki mice fed cholesterol.
source: The mRNAs encoding SREBP-1c and two other LXR targets, ABCG5 and ABCG8, were enhanced in WT and Ubiad1Ki/Ki mice fed cholesterol (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
